lines.text: Three computers agree. Could all three still be wrong?
Machines we trust with lives don't rely on one computer. They run three and take a vote. If one goes wrong, the other two outvote it.
lines.source: triple modular redundancy with a majority voter

lines.text: For the vote itself to fail, two have to go wrong at the same moment. If their faults are unrelated, that almost never happens. And the more computers you add, the rarer it gets.
lines.source: binomial tail: the vote fails only when a majority fails, P = 3q^2(1-q) + q^3, and falls as q^(m+1) with more channels

lines.text: But there's a condition hiding in that. Unrelated. Give every computer the same flaw, and they fail together. The vote is unanimous, and wrong. Adding more copies changes nothing.
lines.source: common-cause (beta-factor) failure: the floor rho*q does not depend on the number of channels

lines.text: June, 1996. Ariane 5 lifts off on its first flight, steered by two navigation computers: one active, one backup. Identical machines, identical software.
lines.source: Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report, Sec. 1.1, 2.1 (two SRIs, identical hardware and software, one active, one hot stand-by)

lines.text: The software came from an older, slower rocket. On the new one, a number grew too big for the space it had been given. The backup shut itself down. A moment later the active one did the same, for the same reason.
lines.source: Sec. 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 finding p (software reused from Ariane 4; horizontal velocity builds five times faster; unprotected 64-bit to 16-bit conversion; back-up failed one 72 ms cycle before the active unit)

lines.text: The rocket took the error message for flight data, swerved hard, and tore itself apart, about forty seconds into the flight.
lines.source: Sec. 2.1 (diagnostic bit pattern interpreted as flight data; full nozzle deflections; break-up at about H0 + 39 s)

lines.text: Nothing had broken. Both computers were healthy, and both did exactly what their software said. A backup that shares your mistake is not a backup.
lines.source: Sec. 2.2 (the switch-off of two still healthy critical units; the same software runs in both)

lines.text: So the cure is not more copies. It's different ones: built by different teams, in different ways, so their mistakes don't line up. That lowers the risk. It never makes it zero.
lines.source: design diversity lowers common-mode risk without removing it (old lab film, scene 6)

lines.text: We are handing more decisions to machines that check each other, and now to AI. The question is never how many agree. It's whether they can all be wrong at once.
lines.source: the author's view (old lab film, closing caption)
